title: Article 21 — Protection of life and personal liberty

content.overview: Article 21 of the Constitution of India provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. HISTORICAL reading after A.K. Gopalan treated the clause in a narrow, compartmentalised way. CURRENT law after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India requires that the procedure be fair, just and reasonable, and reads Article 21 with Articles 14 and 19 where those articles are engaged (often called the golden triangle). Life is more than animal existence; personal liberty is a residual freedom subject only to lawful and fair procedure. Always verify the official constitutional text and the specific statute or executive act under challenge.

sections.heading: Study treatise — meaning and foundation
sections.body:
Topic at a glance
Article 21 is the central guarantee against arbitrary deprivation of life and personal liberty. It does not freeze a closed list of rights. It sets a constitutional standard: deprivation is permitted only through procedure established by law, and that procedure must meet fairness under current doctrine.

Text (verify on India Code / official text)
"No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."

Why the rule exists
A written constitution that enumerates freedoms still needs a residual protection when the State acts against the body, movement, or conditions of living of a person. Article 21 is that residual shield. It binds the State under Article 12.

"Procedure established by law" — historical and current
HISTORICAL: In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras the dominant approach treated Article 21 as satisfied by a procedure prescribed in a valid enacted law, with limited cross-reading of Articles 14 and 19 into preventive-detention challenges of that era.
CURRENT: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India holds that procedure established by law cannot be arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; it must be fair, just and reasonable. Where Articles 14 and 19 are also engaged, the articles are read together rather than in sealed compartments.

"Life" and "personal liberty"
"Life" under current doctrine is not limited to mere animal existence. Courts have recognised dimensions connected with dignity and living conditions in decided cases. Do not invent new free-standing rights without authority; always tie the claim to deprivation by the State and to procedure.
"Personal liberty" is a wide residual concept of freedom of the person, subject to procedure established by law that meets the fairness standard.

Legal foundation
Constitution of India, Part III, Article 21. Related: Articles 14, 19, 20, 22. Doctrines: golden triangle; procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. Primary text source: India Code / Legislative Department official text.

sections.heading: Essential ingredients (Track A)
sections.body:
1. A person (citizen or non-citizen — Article 21 is not limited to citizens).
2. Deprivation of life or of personal liberty (identify the concrete deprivation).
3. The actor is the State within the meaning of Article 12 (or an authority held to be State).
4. The State relies on a procedure said to be established by law.
5. CURRENT test: that procedure must be fair, just and reasonable; arbitrariness fails Article 21 and often Article 14.
6. Where Articles 14 and/or 19 are engaged, examine the golden-triangle interaction.
7. Remedies typically run under Article 32 (Supreme Court) or Article 226 (High Courts) — see related topics.

sections.heading: How the rule operates
sections.body:
Identify the deprivation (detention, passport impoundment, restriction on movement, conditions affecting life and dignity as recognised in authority).
Identify the legal source the State invokes (statute, rules, executive order).
Map the procedure actually followed against the procedure prescribed.
Ask whether the procedure is fair, just and reasonable under Maneka.
If Articles 14 or 19 are also in play, apply those standards together with Article 21.
Distinguish preventive detention (also engage Article 22) from ordinary criminal process (engage BNSS / historical CrPC as applicable, plus Article 21 fairness).
Do not treat BNSS or BSA as repealing Article 21; they supply ordinary procedure, which itself must satisfy Article 21.

sections.heading: Distinctions and misconceptions
sections.body:
Article 21 vs Article 19: Article 19 lists specific freedoms for citizens; Article 21 is residual personal liberty and life for every person.
Article 21 vs Article 22: Article 22 adds specific safeguards for arrest and preventive detention; Article 21 remains the general fairness floor.
Article 21 vs Article 20: Article 20 addresses ex post facto criminal law, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination — related but distinct.
Trap: Writing that any enacted procedure automatically satisfies Article 21. Correction: CURRENT law requires fairness, justice and reasonableness.
Trap: Treating Gopalan as the sole current test. Correction: State the historical position and the Maneka shift.
Trap: Inventing a new fundamental right without case or textual anchor. Correction: Frame the interest as part of life or personal liberty only with authority.
Trap: Saying criminal codes replace Article 21. Correction: Ordinary procedure is still measured against Article 21.

sections.heading: Track B — chamber and litigation anchors
sections.body:
Forum: Supreme Court under Article 32 for enforcement of Part III; High Courts under Article 226 for rights and legality of State action. Criminal trial forums apply ordinary procedure (BNSS for post-commencement procedure where applicable; historical CrPC for saved matters under Section 531 BNSS — verify dates).
Pleadings: Identify the person, the exact deprivation, the instrument of power, the procedure followed step-by-step, and the fairness defect (arbitrariness, absence of hearing where required, disproportionate measure, ultra vires step).
Evidence: Constitutional claims still need facts. Burden allocation follows the BSA (including ss. 104–106 patterns) and any special statute. Electronic records engage BSA s. 63 certificate requirements where applicable.
Limitation: Writs are discretionary; delay and laches matter. Statute-specific limitation applies to ordinary civil/criminal remedies.
Core submissions (illustrative structure, not a script):
- Petitioner/accused: deprivation + absence of fair procedure / ultra vires / arbitrariness.
- State: valid law + procedure followed + reasonableness and public interest.
Order sought: quashing of order, production/release, mandamus to follow fair procedure, or consequential directions — framed to the concrete deprivation.

sections.heading: Revision points
sections.body:
Art. 21 = no deprivation of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law.
CURRENT: procedure must be fair, just and reasonable (Maneka).
HISTORICAL: Gopalan-era narrow reading — state as history, not as sole current test.
Golden triangle: Arts. 14, 19, 21 read together where engaged.
"Person" includes non-citizens for Article 21.
Pair with Arts. 20 and 22 for criminal process; pair with Arts. 32 and 226 for remedies.
Verify official text; do not invent holdings or paragraph numbers.

examples.title: Example — fair procedure required
examples.body: An authority impounds a passport under a statutory power but gives no meaningful opportunity to be heard where the statute and fairness require one. CURRENT Article 21 analysis examines whether the procedure actually followed was fair, just and reasonable, not only whether a statute exists on paper.

examples.title: Example — historical vs current framing
examples.body: An answer that cites only Gopalan to say any enacted procedure is enough is incomplete under CURRENT law. State Gopalan as historical, then apply Maneka’s fairness standard and, where relevant, Articles 14 and 19.

examples.title: Example — section not a substitute for facts
examples.body: Counsel asserts a vague ‘violation of Article 21’ without identifying the deprivation, the State actor, or the procedure used. The claim is not trial-ready. Article 21 is applied to concrete deprivations through identified procedure.

hypotheticals.question: A statutory regulator suspends a professional licence without supplying the material relied upon and without a hearing, though the statute contemplates an inquiry. The professional approaches the High Court. How should Article 21 be framed alongside other provisions?
hypotheticals.analysis: Identify the deprivation (livelihood and liberty interests as recognised in authority — do not expand beyond supported doctrine). Identify the State character of the regulator if contested under Article 12. Map the procedure used against the statutory inquiry and the Maneka fairness standard. Engage Article 14 if the action is arbitrary. Remedies under Article 226 may include quashing and remand for fair procedure. Applicable frame: Articles 12, 14, 21 and the parent statute; verify facts and text before filing.
